text: In the gathering, one person appears pale-faced and calm, and like bees around honey, both young and old cluster around him. A sword hangs at his waist, and a shield at his side. Before his knees, two bareheaded men sit kneeling, offering cups and receiving dark beer in large goblets. – Drink, Mindia, – they say, – it is good beer, fit for drinking; tell us something, by God’s grace, some proper Georgian verse.
– What did the drunk man tell you, men? Wine overpowered his mind; let the saying remain for tomorrow, if death allows me. – He lifted the karakhan, drained it, and emptied it.
Being back from captivity, he delighted in being among his brothers; like many others, he too would get drunk on beer.
They told unbelievable stories about this Mindia: it is said that Mindia had been held captive by the kajis for twelve years.

Captivity had greatly oppressed him, being outside his homeland; time passed, many Easters and Nativities went by, but Mindia’s captivity did not come to an end. Slavery had worn down his heart; his soul longs to rise. He remembered his snow-covered mountains, the darkened gorges, the uneven roads, his mother, father, and brothers mourning his fate, his poor little hut, which he would have taken as paradise, and many times he had fervently prayed to the icons and to God for help.

At last he said: “I shall kill myself; such a life is worse than this!” For the devils, Kobia found a meal set on the fire. He knew that they boiled snakes and often ate them; the devils, by their devilry, endured taking snakes into their mouths, and he thought to himself that this would turn into a torment for him.

He took one piece, and with disgust, like a thief, ate it, and at that moment heaven, with a merciful eye, looked down upon the captive: a new soul was breathed into him, a new flesh was put on him; the sight of the heart and of the eyes, like that of a blind man and a deaf man, was opened. From this day on he understands everything that birds sing, or plants and animals, when they rejoice and when they suffer. Whatever the Lord has created, whether animate or inanimate, all of it, it turns out, has a language; there has been no lawless one.

He feels this himself too, and is astonished at the change in the nature of the captive. He understood that the serpent’s eating was a dream sent by the demons. They showed wisdom as a serpent, so that it would loathe it as food, though “You too, eat it, Mindia,” they did not hesitate to say.

He is swift as a bullet, cunning as a serpent; all of Pshav-Khevsureti worships him and sees him as a comfort, and crowned Tamar is always saying this:

“Only let Mindia be with me, and with him the mountain folk are a people; however much the enemy may strive, he can do me no harm.”

He knows the trick for defeating and crushing the foe; if he reaches the wounded while they are still alive, there is no need to fear death.  
His incomparable remedy heals even one cut in half; thus his forces never diminish in war, for he always has a great army.  
Far and wide has the tale of his adventures gone.

II. When spring arrives, the land awakens: lightness and joy stroll everywhere. The first shoots appear, flowers cling to the green, and Mindia roams eagerly through mountain and field. He greets every plant and herb with a salutation; nature too cries “Hurrah!” with its richly adorned banner, flowers, with necks outstretched, painted as if by a brush, all raise a hum in unison: “Long live Mindia!” Trees shake their leaves, nature begins to rustle, and then each one in turn starts to whisper: “I am the remedy for t h i s”; another cries out — “f o r t h a t”; Mindia plucks them too and carries them away, while morning dew still lies upon them.

It turns out that flowers have a nature of their own: only to heal the sick do they care; bodies luxuriant with life they disregard. They are meant for delight, for human benefit, for the broken bones and flesh. Such is the nature of flowers, and it seems trees too have their own sorrow; only Mindia can hear their groaning and complaint. Because of this, his life is greatly burdened: he went to a tree with an axe and said, “I must cut this one down!” He struck the axe, and at that moment the tree’s groan was heard: “Do not kill me, my Mindia, do not darken my sun; because I am unarmed, do you therefore mock me as a tree?!” His arms grow weak, and he stares blankly at the sky. He turns to another tree, and it begins to groan even more. He returns empty-handed, unable to bring back firewood, and so that the fire does not go out on the ashes, he lights hay or straw, dried stalks, and adds brushwood; if he finds any dry twigs anywhere, he does not reject them either. Still he thanks God, still, in the evening and in the morning.

He advises others too: “Men, come, let us not commit sin; do not cut down the tree, let us be content with the branches, with a little dry brushwood.” No one listens; they call his advice nonsense: “God has created it for our benefit, for our use!” And even today no one spares the poplar-beech tree from being killed.

III. When he begins reaping the field, he is mad, deranged: he cuts off one foot here, another there, with his heart torn out; he tramples the whole field, tears it up, lays it waste, as long as he has strength in his arm, he spins like a top, and when he grows exhausted, he sprawls out on the ground.

If you ask: “Why do you do this?”  
he will answer you thus: “What are you saying, men? You do not understand, and that is why you blame my conduct.  
Do you not know how the ears beg me? You should know, you should see the ears’ necks bending,  
when ten thousand of them thunder together from every side,  
and when I am with the sickle in hand, they see me as their god:

‘No, cut me, Mindi, do not leave me, by your groans!’  
‘No, me,’ another cries, ‘the sky frightens me more.  
If I see even a little cloud, I collapse in body.  
Alas, if hail should come, it will cut my throat with a knife.’  
Another cries even more: ‘Do not spare me, rejoice in your own strength!’

They drive me mad with their pleading, I go out of my mind with their complaints:  
I try, and with my two hands and eyes I cannot reach them all,  
and in the meantime I myself become one who must be turned back by water.

In the field, hail is feared — that men may be left without sustenance;  
for how can hail, like a sickle, destroy anything else?  
For the good of men, the ears preserve themselves, golden in color;  
they do not wish to rot uselessly, to be pecked by crows and vultures.  
That is why they hurry to the harvest, all crying out together;  
they wish to become bread, to be eaten, so that the hungry may be fed —  
let us speak of the dead men’s memorial, let us mention the powers of the heavens.

IV. They had a feast day, the drinking of beer, a revelry. The great worshipper is invited by the feast day of Gudani Jvari. The people are convinced; the elders discuss many things: some speak of others’ affairs, others of their own adventures; they speak of bravery, of guns and of swords, of who wears a chain-cutting belt around the waist—everyone praised that one. They listen reverently to what each person says from experience. At the same time, they began a discussion about the knowledge of the serpent-eater, the woodcutter, the grass-mower, and the sin of their deeds.

Chalkhia says to the assembly: “I am surprised by your thinking; I have told you many times before, and I will say the same now: if trees and stones had tongues, why would we not have heard it? Minia has invented a lie to deceive us. Are we not men like him? Do we not also have ears, I wonder?! I do not say this in secret; it reaches his own ears too. If I am not speaking the truth about this, let him think it in his own heart. Let us say pity is good for trees, stones, grass, animals… But killing a man outweighs all else, even if he is an enemy of all. Then we should no longer kill men either, I tell you, listen to what I say: I have seen, in the enemy’s case, a man cut down by a sword, and Minia standing on a hill. Why does he do this? After all, the law does not permit us to kill, but we kill those who destroy our peace, or take our land, or our wives, or prevent us from knowing the law. Then even God will not count it as sin if we turn our hand against the enemy; likewise, so long as we live, let us cut down the beech and the elm.”

– He is not lying, no, Chalkhia, Mindia is the one who is lying, exactly, he has piled up a thousand kinds of lies right before our eyes, like a heap, – some people in the crowd were saying timidly, in a low voice.

– If we follow that thought, then, my enemy, how could we live? Why should we know what is not meant to be known from the Lord?! He who instructs the people on that is doing very badly. From the good we always have hope of help and relief, and not of our destruction, of harm to our lives!.. – This was the conclusion reached by the Khevsur assembly…

Mindia was sitting right there, tears streaming from his eyes.  
No one knew what it was that pained his heart.  
His eyes were fixed in one direction; he heard nothing of the people around him.  
He came back to himself when Berdia said to him:  
– Why do you not listen to us, Mindia? I wonder what it is you are crying for?  
This does not surprise me from you, nor is it surprising from anyone else —  
to change mourning and weeping into joy nine times in a single moment.  
– And the whole band of Khevsurs turned their faces toward Mindia…

– Well then, say it, – Bardia asks again, – what sorrow weighs on your heart? – I’m listening to those birds, – he pointed at the birds with his finger; two of them, wings drooping, were sitting on the stones beneath the ash tree. – One is telling the other the story of death to its children; the one sitting on the left is the mother, and on the right is the storyteller—your enemy, for a parent, heartbroken, is weeping for its children.

The birds are only now being watched; the Khevsur gathering is complete.  
One of the birds, at that very moment, as if overcome by sleep,  
fell down from the rock and gave up its soul.  
Which of the two died—this is a matter of law!

The Khevsurs looked at one another with astonished eyes;  
could such a deed truly be done by human power?  
They became convinced of that knowledge; the matter lay before them all,  
but what the heart has sensed, the mind can help with nothing.  
They mow grass, they kill beasts, they light the hearth with firewood.  
Who could be made to hate chicken meat, tell me yourselves, you foxes?!  
Who would sit down on embers if they did not see the log above them?!

V. Many times they desired to campaign against the Lezgi-Persians, the Kists, and the Turks;  
the victorious men always come to Khevsureti.  
The rampart of Kartli grew strong;  
they spread a shroud over the enemy.  
If a people is the conqueror of its foes,  
it needs nothing more than that.  
As long as Mindia is the leader,  
nothing can harm the Khevsurs;  
no one dares to challenge them anymore,  
there is peace everywhere…  
Blessed is he to whom the country is grateful.

VI. On the top of the sheer cliff stood a house,  
its roof leaning against the sky; all around were huge mountains,  
raised up in their full height,  
plastered over with snow,  
unyielding in their strength.  
If you see them once like that,  
you always want to behold them with your eyes.  
They are even more beautiful when they are clothed in green.  
Even if the sun settles on their breast,  
and avalanches rush down with thunder,  
the ravines cough, like the sick with consumption,  
yet their beauty is consecrated by heaven.  
Many a time a cool wind circles above them with a sigh.  
In summer, black clouds light candles with a spark.  
There, indeed, no one plows with a plow,  
nor does anyone sow anything with seed;  
only the chamois walk on the cliffs, sharpening their horns.  
And the stern cliffs, grim-faced,  
with roots sunk into the abyss,  
think neither of the soul,  
nor grow fat on carrion,  
without greeting, without caress,  
peering out from the rock.

A tower is attached to the house,  
blackened with smoke,  
day and night shaken by the firing of jezairs.  
What will give the poor one rest,  
while enemies are all around,  
while the desire for revenge has been planted in the hearts of mankind,  
and many a bullet fired by the enemy has struck his chest!

From the house comes the sound of quarrel, the voice of argument and anger; there are not many people there — the tone of conversation is that of two. A fire is lit upon the hearth, blazing with firewood; on the far side a woman is seen beside the children, and here a lone Khevsur laments much of something with sighing.

(Husband) May that day turn black, the day I took you as my wife.  
Before that, I had no man on earth as my equal.  
I became completely ruined because of you, wretched one, helpless and foul.  
What am I? Am I still a man, worthy to walk beneath the sky?!  
I remain only what I was before; if only I knew a remedy!..  
My life is worthless, today I am worse than a black cliff’s stone,  
I suffer an incurable affliction because of you; before the Lord, I have sinned because of you.  
Even my children have become a burden to me; they have changed my thoughts.  
For my lost soul and body, I now weep day and night.

(Wife) Why do you blame me for your own fault, when you came home by force?  
You did not let me go on my way, and you filled me with sin and blame:  
“Mzia, I love you very much,” you said, scattering tears from your eyes,  
and for the sake of my heart, you came home to my brothers with a sword.  

Why was the sweet sugar of before made bitter now?  
Or why do you mourn having children, why do you speak of complaint against God?!  
Who would cast away his own wife and child for another’s?  
Why do you make us the reason for the change in your mood?

**(Husband)** Because, foolish woman, you kept complaining, lamenting: “The cold is killing the children,” you cried like a bereaved mother: “How much firewood does Berdia have, what a fire he lights, go and see,” and you held up fools as examples for life. You spoke of things to be said to the heart in my Georgian hearing, you longed for a good life, and you baked poisoned bread. And I, little by little, day by day, slowly and gradually, began to turn back to my own belief, with cunning: today I cut down one tree, though many begged me: “Why are you doing that, Mindia, as if you were not an enemy?!” Tomorrow I cut down two, and thus I steeled my heart like stone, so that I would feel nothing at all, and I asked God for strength. You longed for deer meat, if only you had heard of anyone’s killing; how many times has this complaint pierced my heart and chest: “Young men raised without meat, what manliness will they show? I have never heard of anyone raised so by another man.” Ah, why did the earth not swallow you up before saying this!.. I followed too — I killed game, fattened and delighted by the carcasses, you rejoiced with your children, and I was left with a splitting head. It would have been better to be struck by lightning than to become like this; once lost, I can no longer find it by any means.
(Spouse) And what hardship is it of yours, that you pain yourself so forcibly; why do they not count chopping wood, hunting beasts, and the like as blame?

(husband) You do not know, no, you thin-minded one, chatterer, over-sensitive fool, one who knows the pleasantness of this world! It is not worth it—for me to mourn my knowledge and strength, that among them not even one, fool, remains anywhere with me?! It is not fitting that the dead should know their own death—if one is dead, let him mourn himself; is his own existence not dreadful? Find me another existence, more bitter than this, to compare with! Such a dead man today am I; what hardship is there for other dead ones in being dead! They are at rest, they feel nothing with feeling. How then can I be of use to the world, when I have been emptied of knowledge: the flowers tell me nothing, nor do I have any awareness of them; would there be anything more for a man than to expose himself to danger? I no longer hear the birds, I no longer hear the field, and since then I have not heard the sweet greeting of the green. This is nothing; in other ways too I am no longer of any use; whether I lie here in the mountains or go down to the plain, no one will buy my ugly face for straw. I can no longer serve the world in the army that repels the enemy, because I no longer have the former understanding in my head. Why did my star not vanish quickly in the sky! Until today enemies could not move from within the house to the gate in fear, and if they hear this, they will come and turn us to dust; they will turn our houses, fortresses, and towers into ruins. Alive I will not see this; your day too is ended, from you I have lost my mind, I have sold the holy faith… Now let me destroy the world too, while you have breath in your mouths!.. Or why do I need life, or why should I bring you back to life, if my whole being will no longer be sound?! Or with what face should I live here? How can I justify myself before God? I am disgraced before everyone—before the living and before the dead. Why then do I need armor, why do I need a sword, if the blow struck against my enemy will no longer have strength?! The offspring of this earth, my debt and obligation, how then can I eat bread, how can I drink water?!

He rose and, with folded arms, stood at the doorway.  
When he looked at the high mountains, he sighed bitterly.  
The mountains have dried up; streams come rushing down headlong,  
In the ravines the avalanche has thinned, like the remains of a dragon.  
Clear raindrops sparkle on the heather,  
On the fields the flowers shine — Queen Tamar’s eyes.  
To the one who has come to the edge of the cliff, I would give my heart and breast to the sun!..  
The travelers from the far side of the mountain have crossed over unharmed.  
The mountain slopes are adorned with sheep and cattle, like moles on a beautiful woman;  
The mountain and plain, tormented by winter, have come back to life.  
There are many wretches in the world, many to be pitied;  
If we see one, our eyes cannot see many others!

There is commotion in the villages, great is the shouting and uproar: “Let it be made known where the serpent-eater Mindia is; the Kists are coming with an army, they have broken the bridge over the Argun, to meet the enemy, men, now it depends on us!”

Great preparations were made, the people were surging like the sea; whichever way you looked, rifles and swords were flashing. For a long time the Khevsurs had no longer been cutting down the enemy’s detachments, no longer trampling mercilessly over their devastated camp; famished for war, they could scarcely wait for dawn. Everyone had this in their heart: who will kill the leader first, cut off his head and right hand, and return home in glory? At the shrine, with candles, the cup of honor will be offered to him. His name too will remain forever worthy of praise.

In the fortress-towers the women and children were gathered; they had prepared the packs and provisions for their husbands and sons.

VIII. It is getting dark. The dark ravines are becoming black. They seem to the eye as though they have fallen ill. The high mountains, the cliffs, the proud Aragvi itself — all are sad; I see them silently weeping. Only the bold messengers cry out village to village: “Whoever is missing from the army tomorrow shall be uprooted from the ground!”

No fire is seen anywhere outside, no shepherd’s whistle is heard;  
No more have they left needle-thimbles at the door.  
In the village, everyone has settled down; tower-fortresses shelter them,  
They hide sheep and cattle, and hidden treasures in secret places.

A faint light would appear a little in the Khakhmati shrine,  
candles burned on the ridge, the flame met the mist,  
at times it would shine out at dawn, and at times it would dim,  
it would fade away; it was like a soul-struggling sick man,  
dying in torment and woe.
No other son of man is seen there; two men are sitting on the plain, one holding a bloodied dagger, with blood on his hands; before them lies a slaughtered calf, resting on its side.

Berdia (the khevisberi): May grace be given to you, Mindia, for that heart and that conduct, for the thoughts with which you offer sacrifice and place your hope in God; may your name never fail you, so long as the sword is girded at your waist. Hope of Khevsureti, may the Cross be merciful to you; may it always lead you victorious and bring your army with you and for you! I think, for the tenth year now, you have slaughtered, you have destroyed cattle; why do you beg for so much, what is it that you have done wrong? One rule is enough, even two; your entreaty is excessive. May I not offend God by what I have now uttered.
(Mindia) I still have a whole herd of oxen, three or four cows; I’ll name them too, if only my sores would heal.
(Berdia) What ulcer, man? We’ve never heard of you having an ulcer; you heal thousands of others who have ulcers, I think.

(Mindia) It’s a different matter, Berdia, I cannot say that easily: we men cannot speak of our own defeat, we are quicker to speak of another’s. Those who have money, if you know, do they not open their purses everywhere? Tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, you will hear it when the messenger comes from the mountain.

(Berdia) You are our hope, and the fortune of the Khevsurs is with you. We believe, and you too know, that you speak with God; and the icon follows you as a victor, as everyone knows well. May the fortune never fail you by the power of Saint George; may the Lord never abandon us, nor shield us with His cloak. He took the cup in his hand and again Berdia began:

“Glorious Saint George, and merciful one, yours are they!.. May you help me, for all the icons the Lord has created, you are my protector; may not a single living one be left to me. If tomorrow, or the day after tomorrow, we are surely to have war with the enemy, while you are alive with us, what can they do to us?!”

When he said this, the eyes of the one praying filled with hot tears; lest anyone notice, he turned away and wiped them with his hand. He fell down before the army, like a beast cut down by a scythe, or like brushwood, or a twig to be bent. He prays with tear-filled eyes; the meaning of the prayer cannot be heard. Berdia had never before seen anyone praying so fervently—this is what he finds strange: it is more like the torment of mourning than a calm request for mercy. Tears flow, quiet sobbing mingles with the clatter of armor; he prays, kneeling, and many hours pass.

“Hear me, Cross of Khakhmati!” he himself adds: “Do not make my supplication vain; guide me toward what is good.”

IX. At midnight the deluge began, the torrents burst forth, they broke, as if the doors in the rocky ravines had been, and they did not bring to the plain the mountain’s entrusted message. Often the dewdrops of the clouds of grass were laid upon it; the candles on the rocks of Khakhmati have vanished and no longer flicker. Nowhere is the khevisberi seen, nor the praying mourner; only the crow of the military camp glares out angrily, and the Aragvi, weary and shouting, is breaking the cliffs.

X. At dawn, with wings folded, after a night of tears,  
the mists slept on the mountains, their heads wrapped in cloth;  
sometimes they gladden us with the life-giving dew,  
other times they make us curse our fate with the evil of what has been done.  
Below, the meadows and ravines, yesterday full of avalanche,  
today rejoice in life, brightened with green,  
and the tower, deep in thought, gazes down upon the valley from above.

In the tower, women can be seen, like flowers of the mountain; they defeat the enemy, if not the Khevsurs — that is their talk. Through the loopholes they gaze restlessly over the meadow and implore for their army the power of God and the icon. From here the surroundings are clearly visible: the mountain, every mountain pass; no insect can hide from a man’s eye, nor any beast. Some sit on a plank, deliberating, while knitting a stocking; they too speak of the homeland and recite a holy prayer.

Sandua (woman), Mziav, with a broken heart you are more than others;  
If you grieve for your husband, tearful-eyed, you cannot be consoled for his death;  
you do not know that in war he counts it as his own fate,  
and no mother has yet raised the slayer of Mindia.  

Then what am I to do? Many of mine have gone to the army:  
my husband, my three brothers, none have been spared from the company.  
No one can outdo your husband; he will do as he has always done,  
as many times before, so now too he will bring harm to the enemy:  
whoever he has slain, that one will slay a horned deer like an ox.

(Mzia) Alas, when he could no longer be a boy, he used to see such dreams: for a whole year he seemed ill, gnawing at his own flesh with his teeth. “I will slaughter wife and children,” he would say, though for some reason he did not dare to do it. He leaned on the icons and God, made offerings; wherever our livestock was, he would come and not even eat bread, though I invited him many times. I saw him alone many times, quietly, crying like a child: “I have lost a precious treasure,” he would say to himself. He would sit on the roof all night, staring at the sky, and to those who came and went he would say nothing at all; he no longer wanted visitors either, and not us either—could grief have turned his hair and beard gray in such a short time?! Many times I watched him secretly in the dark, quietly, but I could not bring myself to bear his being alone. That he cried for himself and for people, I understood completely: “I can no longer be of use to the world,” he would cry in secret. As for wife and children, especially in the later days, he would turn toward us with hostility.

(Sandua) We have not heard that; I hear it for the first time from you:  
I think you are like Minda, comparable to the sun.  
For that, no matter how much you boast, the country will not believe you.  
I wonder why what was said to you was not boasted to others?  
As if he were mourning some knowledge, complaining about some knowledge?  
Or what were you guilty of?..  
Was his heart hurting so much that, to kill his wife and children,  
he reached for the sword with his hand?!

(Mzia) So, she was saying, as the sun shone on them, “I did not speak falsely —” she laid a hand on her children, both of them standing by her side — “that I entered into sin because of you, and did what should not be done: I cut firewood, I killed beasts, as if it were nothing. The flowers no longer speak to me, nor do the stars at night. The great knowledge and strength granted to me by the Lord I have lost by following you; why then does the sword strike my waist? And a thousand other such things she hurled at me with foam at her mouth, and two or three times I escaped, she nearly killed me with a gun. Perhaps she still had hope, she prayed to the icons, she worked… and she pitied us too, and that is why she did not kill us.”

(Sandua) If what you said is true, then you have fallen into sin; that tongue of yours should be cut off, you should be hung up high by a hook, and a fire should be lit beneath you, so that you burn in its flames: you have brought the world into sin, while we are by its power!

(Mzia) Yes, if I am guilty of something, I would deserve punishment; why should it be considered a sin that I gave thought to labor? If a man needs a wife and children, he must also have the means to support them. We know our own business; what do we women understand of armor… He himself should have thought of it, a man is a man for that reason: if he has not harmed or robbed another for the sake of one, why should the innocent, the one who has done no sin, be blamed? Why should one’s sin be borne by another — when was that ever said to be a virtue? Still, he felt something bad; that is what the poor man was troubled by, foreseeing the matter before it happened. Last night too I had a bad dream; what may happen, I wonder?!
(Sandua) What did you see, Mziava, tell me, perhaps it will come true well and may the Lord not make us lose what we have to drink and lose?

(Mzia) I saw a terrible thing, Sandua, dreadful, heart-rending, soul- and body-disturbing, mind-revolting: torrents had rushed in, like demons breathing hard, and were tearing through mountains and plains; there was a clamor, a roar, like the collapse of heaven and earth, such a rumbling was heard. The peaks of the mountains were breaking off, falling down into the ravines below; along with the mountains, the cliffs too were bursting like guns. The sky looked like tar, blackly seething, hissing, raining tar upon the earth, hot drops falling, and the torrents again flowed horribly, relentlessly. “Help us, we are perishing,” people were crying from all sides.

Indeed I see that people are bringing water, shields, swords;  
from a thousand places the fortress is breaking, and by the Kav fortress there is a house;  
so much misery, and only a mourner is lacking.  
We thought we were not suffering, that we were unharmed,  
but in the end I saw that with house and home we too were cast out.

A flood came rushing from above, tore away the fortress’s foundation,  
and carried it down too, to the gravel bank of the Aragvi.  
It took the house as well, from the upper part, and swept us along too;  
I wanted to cry out, “Help me!” but I could no longer find my voice.  
I was clutching the children to my breast, asking the holy icons and God for help.  
At the same time I tried to get out, edging toward the bank;  
I was covering the children’s faces with the veil of a black kerchief.  
And every time I reached the shore, there before me stood  
the faces of men, black as pitch.  
They shoved me, threw me into the water, and called out to me:  
“Where are you going? Go on, follow the water; it is God’s command!”

And at that moment I saw that the water in front of us was carrying away our man; he turned back to me and said, in a sweet, gentle voice, “Please forgive me, Mzia, for all the insults I hurled at you and the anger I caused you; what you see befalling me, I deserve it, it is only right, I have brought it upon myself. Please do not mistreat the children; I beg you, take good care of them!”  
May an enemy suffer what I suffered last night—I, who saw such a dream!..
(Sandua) So you couldn’t come out—should I take you?
(Mzia) No… it took us away, Sanduav, mothers and children, all of us.
(Sandua) May no evil befall you; may God keep you whole.

(Voice of the women in unison) They are coming, the host is coming, God, make the sign of the cross!.. Mzia, get up, look, there is your husband, side by side with the banner-bearers, he is the rising moon.

(One woman) There are our boys, may their mother take their place on their shoulders… Alas, how beautiful they are, who would see them among the dead!.. May God never let me see such a thing in my life.
**(The second woman)** Look, my little one is following them over there. How beautifully they are walking, may their mother be exchanged for them in their bosoms!

(An unmarried woman) I take the place of Tothia, I can hardly tell him apart in a crowd. I saw him… only with difficulty did I recognize him by his manner of moving, in his body. The stallion is biting the bit, he is strained in the arm.
(Second Woman) We have Ushiashi too on our side, how he drives Lurja!.. When it comes to the sword, he won’t start dodging either. Then let me see him, when he starts clutching at the shield.
(First woman) I would not see my brother, it would make breathing difficult for me: I would turn my face elsewhere, and begin to close my eyes.

(Second Woman) Not me. I want my brother’s well-being, good life, and good name just as much, Zekhuav, as a candle in the dark, rest and food for the weary and the hungry. It is good that a brother’s well-being is something everyone speaks of.
(First woman) Who wouldn’t want that, beauty, who is so thin-minded? But she is eye-burned, seeing her brother in distress.
(Second woman) Who will give it a name without him, if he does not do what must be done?!
(General voice) God, save us; icons, you who have led the warriors, show them to us unharmed, just as we now behold them.
Many a heart was troubled by a thousand kinds of fear — let no one be surprised, for this comes to us by nature; in fearful times, when we remember a beloved thing, we do so with fear!..

XI. The army lined up on the mountain, gathering on the broad plain. The glitter of guns and weapons matches the sunlight. Rocks torn loose by horses’ hooves roll downhill. Here they held a council on the proper way to meet the enemy: whether to descend onto the plain, or to meet them on the ridge. Everyone stands on their feet, hands resting on their swords. Everyone’s eyes were fixed on Mindia, waiting for his answer: if he said nothing, the Khevsurs would speak with one voice.
(Army) We have always followed your advice, and no harm has come to us. How should we act? Advise us—will your answer be brief?!

(Mindia) I can advise you nothing, Khevsurs, I am no longer fit to be a counselor: that was another time, another wisdom; now my advice would be hard for you to use. Weigh it well, you are an army, gather your thoughts as one. I must fight alone, that is why I came out onto the field; or when has the people ever made me a fool for all time?!

(Army) May God and the icon be angry with anyone who, against your counsel, sets foot to go to war, even if they strike him on the head with a fist: let him die and have his mouth filled with the cold clay of the grave.

(Mindia) It’s fine… What can I do, I did not want to get involved in the council. I will tell you, since you have entangled me in so many oaths and curses. I can advise nothing else: meet the Kists in the poisoned ravine.

An uneasy murmur arose among the horsemen; the place prepared to receive the Kists gave rise to sorrow.  
Still, what can one do?.. Nothing, since they have spoken and sworn, the host cannot refuse; it must go there, to the place Mindiya pointed out as fit for battle, even if not one of them survives, if all remain there, they are dead.

It can no longer be said of them, “They have gone”; they raised the banner before them,  
they step lightly, they resemble falcons in flight,  
and they carried along with them the sunbeam glinting on the spearpoints.

XII. For two days beyond the mountain there has been war, great woe: a most brutal battle, tigers have joined with lions, and a rope of blood has been stretched from the mountain down to the plain. Both will not be seen alike; one shall be granted victory by God.

Five or six Khevsurs, dressed in shammurvi fashion, were bringing a man with his hands tied together by a kabalakhi. They brought him down face-first, threw him onto the plain below, and the enraged men addressed him with reproachful words.

(Hevsurs together) Man, why are you killing yourself on purpose, do you desire a forced death? When you push into the enemy’s army, don’t you see what they are doing?! Until now we have trampled them; now they are trampling us, and maybe, Mindia, we should sort out something else—we’ll try, since night has already caught up with us, so that we may exert ourselves tonight.

The captive grinds his teeth and tries to free his hands,  
He struggles long, rolling about, scorched by the worm.  
He longs to die with his brothers; they remain no longer whole,  
It is hard for them, and there is no army left to come to their aid.

Night had also grown deep; the captive had fulfilled his desire, both hands were freed, he rose to his feet, weary, and at that moment he saw fires in the villages — a bad omen. He understood what had happened; he no longer wanted the diviner. He dried up, turned pale, yet no tears came to his eyes; all of it had gathered in his heart and scattered into his arms… He removes his hat… he could no longer speak a word, touched the hilt of the sword with his thumb, drew it out with the scabbard, and pressed its point to his heart. From his chest blood poured forth like a spring, in a rushing stream; the moon also shone down over the ridge of the cattle pens and stared at the self-murderer with the color of a mourning woman…

Even the breeze came and went carelessly, with a soft song…  
It brushed the tip of the sword with its tongue,  
the raised sword, reddened with the crimson juice of a man’s breast,  
and it danced upon the green, merrily, in revelry, whistling.
